chapter: Billy Pierce Studio and New York tap
title: Chuckles as teacher and straight man
summary: J. D. explained steps and Green demonstrated them, which Powell liked; Green was the outgoing one and J. D. the cool straight man.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: So then you two were both -- was Chuckles also teaching at the studio?
No, no. They'd have one -- they wouldn't realize -- they didn't know -- I mean -- that he was such a

great tap dancer, see, because I could ask him a question. He would sit down and explain to me, and he would ask -- he would tell me, say, 'Now try; see how you like it,' you know. If I would do it correctly, he would sit there. If I'd do it incorrectly, he would get up and show me how to do it correctly, you see.

But it was always a process of me trying to demonstrate what he'd say, see, and that's how Eleanor Powell happened to see me over there demonstrating what Chuckles said -- I mean Slim just explained to me what to do, you see. And she liked the rhythm of it. That's how she preferred my type of sounds, tap dancing, you know, so --
Were you also the more verbal of the two? Were you more outward, outgoing than he was?
Yes, I was. See, 'cause he was -- he was more experienced. I mean he wasn't -- he wasn't excited about it all as I was, you see.
He was more the cooler half of the duo.
He was more like the straight man in a certain way?
Yeah, he was the straight man. That was him, Chuckles, yeah.
